issues.issue: "Authorized University official" is undefined, so the class of persons who may demand identification has no stated boundary. The reciprocal duty ("must provide identification if the student requests it") also carries no consequence for non-compliance.

"Replaced as soon as possible" sets no measurable deadline, and the "fee to replace a lost card" is left unquantified. A student's obligation therefore cannot be judged breached on the face of the text.

The parenthetical list of privileges ends in "etc.," a catch-all sitting against enumerated specifics that leaves the covered services indeterminate. "Properly entitled" is likewise undefined and points to no source that fixes entitlement.

"Encouraging, enticing, inuencing or enlisting" — particularly "influencing" — has no boundary, and the prohibition extends to "other ofcial University documents" that are nowhere identified. A student cannot tell from the text which documents or what degree of influence is caught.

Section 2.0 is framed as a shared aspiration ("share the responsibility," "requires the cooperation of all") rather than a rule, leaving open whether it is independently enforceable against a student alongside the specific duties in 2.1–2.13. Its status as preamble versus operative standard is contestable.

The prohibited behaviors in 2.1 — "intimidates," "threatens," "harasses," "invades personal privacy" — are single undefined verbs with no severity, intent, or reasonable-person threshold, so their reach is a matter of construction. "Invades personal privacy" in particular has no stated content anywhere in the document.

The closing sentence of 2.1.f permits campus restriction or emergency suspension of "any student involved in such an incident" pending investigation, which cannot be squared with Section 22.2's rule that a student's status shall not be altered pending final action except for "imminent danger." The two set different triggers for the same interim measure.

"If both parties do not consent" is ambiguous between "if either party does not consent" and "if neither consents," and it presumes exactly two participants. The later edition of the same handbook replaces it with "all parties," confirming the phrase was read as defective.

Section 3.0 as written channels sexual misconduct allegations into the ordinary conduct machinery without saying so, while the 2013–2014 handbook's Section 3.0 expressly directs such allegations to the Special Examiner's Process in Section 22.6 "and not the Student Conduct Process found in Section 19." Which process a student is owed for conduct spanning both editions is left unresolved.

"Sexual contact" is nowhere defined and "explicit consent" is qualified only by "may be considered sexual misconduct," so the provision states no determinate rule of prohibited conduct. The gap between "explicit" consent and consent that is merely "clearly communicated" compounds the uncertainty.

3.1's requirement of "explicit consent" cannot be squared with 3.3, which allows consent to be "communicated verbally or through actions" and lack of consent to be "inferred." One provision demands an express manifestation; the other contemplates inference from conduct.

3.2 makes "taking advantage of someone's incapacitation or intoxication" misconduct, but 3.1 provides that only incapacity — not intoxication — destroys the ability to consent. Read together, 3.2 sanctions sexual activity with a person who under 3.1 is capable of consenting, and "taking advantage" is given no content.

3.3's allowance that consent "may be communicated verbally or through actions" and inferred from circumstances cannot be squared with 3.1's requirement of "explicit consent" for each act of sexual contact. A fact-finder applying both has no rule for consent manifested by conduct in an ongoing relationship.
"Students should report" leaves it unclear whether reporting to Public Safety is a duty enforceable under Section 2.2 or merely advisory. Nothing states the consequence of not reporting.

This provision tells a student only that proceedings "may be initiated" through the DSRCS under Sections 3.1–3.3 and 7, without identifying the adjudicative process, while the 2013–2014 handbook removes those same sections from Section 19 and assigns them to the Special Examiner's Process in Section 22.6. The provision therefore cannot be squared with the process actually applied to Section 3 charges.

This summary states that Section 19.8 "permits the passive assistance of legal counsel," but 19.8 itself says such assistance "may be allowed," i.e., is discretionary and conditioned on consulting SRCS staff. The two descriptions of the same entitlement cannot both be right.

The unqualified promise that "the accuser will be informed of the outcome" conflicts with Section 23.O.2, which says final sanction determinations are communicated to the accused "and in some cases to the accuser." Whether outcome disclosure to a sexual-assault accuser is mandatory or discretionary turns on which controls.

"Any reasonably available changes in academic or living situations" is stated only as staff availability to "assist," with no standard for what changes must be made. Whether this creates any entitlement at all is open.

The Title IX Coordinator is identified by the name of a particular individual and telephone number rather than by office, so the provision is inaccurate the moment the officeholder changes (the later handbook names a different coordinator). Whose office holds the Title IX function is then a matter of construction.

"Highest standards of academic integrity" and "other sanctions" state no ascertainable standard or ceiling, while flatly barring a lack-of-understanding defense. The scope of "work that is falsied or is not the result of the student's own effort" is left to the reader.

The sentence requires work "produced without the assistance of others, except for quotation marks, references, and footnotes" — the stated exception is a set of citation devices, not a form of permitted assistance, so the exception does not fit the rule it qualifies. What assistance is actually permitted cannot be read off the words.

The provision permits faculty-authorized joint work and University tutoring, yet makes providing "one's own work to assist another student" an infringement "either knowingly or through negligence," with no carve-out for the authorized collaboration it has just allowed. The negligence standard has no defined content.
"In identical or similar form" gives no measure of how much similarity converts permissible reuse into an infringement. The advisory second sentence does not supply the missing threshold.

5.0 promises "clear policies" and binds sponsors to "the policies outlined below" and to "guidelines for event sponsorship," but the only subsection that follows in this document is 5.5, and the sponsorship guidelines appear nowhere. What a host has agreed to comply with cannot be determined from the instrument as a whole.

"Other drug paraphernalia" is a catch-all appended to "bongs, pipes," and "abuse of legally-obtained drugs" and "misuse of prescription drugs" are undefined. The reach of the prohibition beyond the enumerated items is a matter of construction.

6.2 makes "inappropriate use of property" a violation without defining it, and 6.1's posting ban is drafted as a specific list closing with "etc." The boundary between prohibited and permitted use is left to the administrator.

The protected-category list ends with the open catch-all "any other category protected by law" and contains the garbled entry "qualied special, disabled veteran," so the classes covered cannot be read off the text. The mangled phrase is repeated inconsistently in 7.1 and 7.3.

Harassment is defined by the "purpose or effect of unreasonably interfering" with education or work, or conduct that "otherwise adversely affects" opportunities, with no severity, pervasiveness, or reasonable-person limit. The definition on its face reaches a single subjectively unwelcome act.

The protected-class list in 7.1 ("gender") differs from 7.0 ("gender identity and expression") and from 7.3 ("gender expression"), and 7.3 alone purports to define the defined term "protected class status." Which list governs a charge under Section 7 cannot be settled from one provision.

The bulleted examples — "unwelcome sexual conduct... including offensive comments, touching" and "comments... that would otherwise tend to be degrading" — are introduced by "includes, but is not limited to" and carry no severity threshold. What conduct actually violates the policy is therefore indeterminate.

It is unclear whether the listed examples are independently sanctionable or must also satisfy 7.1's requirement of an intimidating, hostile, or offensive environment that unreasonably interferes with education or work. The two provisions must be read together to know what is prohibited.

The list is expressly "not an exhaustive list," determinations are made "on a case-by-case basis," and the University reserves power to act on conduct "it deems to be inappropriate" regardless of law. No ascertainable standard of prohibited conduct survives those qualifiers.

"In good faith" is the only limit on the protected act and is undefined, and "corrective action up to and including dismissal" states no gradation. Whether a complainant later found to have exaggerated is protected is left open.

"Falsied a claim" is undefined and the provision specifies no process or standard for that determination, sitting uneasily beside 7.4's protection of good-faith complainants. A complaint found unsubstantiated and one found fabricated are not distinguished.

7.6 directs complaints against students to the Office of the Dean of Student Life, while Section 18.0 provides that disciplinary action may be implemented "only though referral of a violation" to the DSRCS. The two routes for the same complaint are not reconciled.

"Other non-University related purposes" is a general catch-all appended to "commercial, political," leaving the prohibited purposes undefined. The cross-reference to Section 13 points to material not set out with this provision.

The provision opens with a historical recital about the 1947 name change that has no operative effect, and a party could argue it colours or limits the permission that follows. The operative grant is confined to "recognized" organizations, leaving unrecognized groups' use unaddressed by negative implication.

The permission is "subject to the standards and policies published elsewhere in this Handbook," without identifying them, and the facilities-use rules referenced are not reproduced. What conditions attach to the permission cannot be determined without material outside the provision.

17.1's guarantee that room and office privacy "must be respected" stands against 17.3, which authorizes periodic staff inspections of residence hall rooms in the student's absence. Whether 17.1 confers any right the University itself is bound by depends on reading the two together.

The search safeguards are made subject to an exception "as outlined in Section 10.5," a section not set out in this document, so the scope of the exception swallowing the rule is unascertainable. The routine inspections authorized by 17.3 also proceed without any statement of permission.

17.3 permits inspections "to check for illegal possession of University-owned property" on 24 hours' public notice, which is a search in substance and cannot easily be squared with 17.2's requirement of advance individualized written permission specifying the rooms and purpose. The line between an "inspection" and a "search" is not drawn.

Access rights are governed by an external "Brandeis University Records Policy" incorporated by reference, whose terms are not in the handbook and may not match the retention and destruction rules in 19.5 and 19.14. Which document controls a student's access to conduct records is unresolved.

The gatekeeping standards — reports "in a timely manner," "insufcient evidence," "the case lacks merit" — are undefined and committed to the administrator's unreviewable judgment. "Timely" fixes no limitation period at all.

18.0 provides that disciplinary action "may be implemented only though referral of a violation" to the DSRCS, which cannot be squared with Sections 22.3 and 22.4, under which the Dean may indefinitely suspend or dismiss a student with no DSRCS referral and with Section 19 expressly inapplicable. The word "only" is contradicted elsewhere in the instrument.

The mediated outcome is said to be "agreed-upon, recorded, nal, and binding," yet 18.2 provides that failure to adhere may expose the party to further mediation or referral to the conduct process. Finality in 18.1 and the continuing exposure in 18.2 cannot both be given full effect.

"Respect of parameters found in Section 21" is garbled and does not identify what limits Section 21 imposes on a negotiated outcome. "Impasse or other impediment" and "educational benet" likewise give the Director an unmeasured discretion.

The record of a mediated outcome is made subject to "the maintenance provisions in Section 19.5," but 19.5 by its terms governs records of administrative action following a finding of responsibility. Whether a mediated, non-disciplinary record is retained and counted as "conduct action" is not answered.

The provision deems a student's silence for 48 hours after "delivery" — including to a campus mailbox or home address — to be "an acceptance of responsibility for the violation," without requiring actual receipt or defining "extenuating circumstances." Responsibility is thereby established by default rather than by evidence.

Where a student fails to choose, 19.1 directs the administrator to "proceed to sanctioning in accordance with Section 19.3," but 19.3 addresses only a student who has chosen administrative action and then missed a meeting. The cross-reference does not supply the sanctioning procedure it invokes.

19.2 defines "class days" to include final exams and Senior Week and to exclude summer instruction, while 19.6 defines the excluded "Summer" differently and adds Study Abroad periods. The same deadline term carries two definitions in adjacent provisions.

Whether a student's absence was "through no fault of her/his own" is left entirely to the same administrator who decides the case, with no criteria stated. The single-reschedule right is thus unmeasurable on the face of the text.

"Pending charges may be discontinued thereafter dependent upon the conduct of the accused student" states no criterion and no decision-maker, and it is unclear whether charges survive the 90-day cap. The sentence can be read either as a promise of dismissal or as unfettered discretion.

The five-year retention rule is stated twice with different triggers — "from the date of the case outcome" and "from the date of the last conduct action involving that student" — and then subjected to an undefined exception for "extraordinary cases as dened by the Dean." The actual retention period cannot be computed from the words.

The 30-class-day hearing deadline is immediately qualified by "or as soon as practicable," which leaves the promised timing without any enforceable limit. The bar on the parties "confronting or questioning the witnesses and accusers... prior to the hearing" is also unbounded in scope and duration.

19.6 says the hearing administrator is non-voting and "will not act in any way to inuence the outcome of a case," which cannot be squared with Section 23.P.1, under which the administrator advises the Board of the accused's past conduct during deliberations, or with 20.11's duty to advise the Board at all stages. The administrator's role is described two incompatible ways.

19.7 lets "the accused and accuser" agree to proceed without the prescribed minimum voting composition, while 20.2 permits waiver of the voting requirements only "by mutual consent of the SCB, the accuser, and the accused." The two provisions specify different consenting parties for the same waiver.

"Passive assistance" is nowhere defined, and the exception permitting "active participation" in "exceptional circumstances" is left to the hearing administrator without criteria. What an adviser may actually do at a hearing is therefore indeterminate.

19.8 makes the passive assistance of legal counsel something that "may be allowed," whereas the Section 3 services statement tells students that this section "permits the passive assistance of legal counsel" whenever parallel criminal charges are pending. The instrument states the same entitlement as both discretionary and as of right.

19.9 says the accuser "must be present at the hearing," but the instrument supplies a consequence only for the accused's absence (19.15 deems acceptance of responsibility) and nowhere states what happens if the accuser does not appear. Read with 19.11's receipt of written testimony from absentee witnesses, the mandatory-presence rule has no ascertainable effect.

19.10 says "the Board shall rule on the admissibility of evidence and any witness testimony" and cross-references 19.6, which instead commits additional or unlisted witnesses "to the discretion of the chairperson of the Board." Who decides what evidence comes in is answered two ways.

The provision guarantees the right to question all witnesses "appearing before the Board and only at the hearing" while in the next breath allowing written testimony from absentee witnesses that by definition cannot be questioned. The right to question and the receipt of untested written statements are stated together without reconciliation.

Placing the "burden of proof" on the accuser cannot be squared with 19.1 and 19.15, which deem responsibility accepted when the accused misses a deadline or a hearing, or with 18.0, under which the University and not the accuser prosecutes the charge. The provision also does not say whether the burden is one of production or persuasion.

The body of 19.13 permits a finding of responsibility "based only upon clear and convincing evidence" while the appended Note substitutes preponderance of the evidence for Section 3 and 7 cases, so the provision states two standards of proof in one breath. Which governs a case charging both a Section 3 violation and other misconduct is unaddressed.

"All decisions shall be made by a majority vote" with the chairperson voting "only to break a tie" cannot be worked with 20.2's four-member academic-integrity panel and 20.5's rule that the SCB is chaired by students. Whether the student chair is one of the required student voters is left unresolved.

The retention sentence is internally inconsistent (five years from the hearing, then five years from the last conduct action) and its parenthetical — "(except in extraordinary cases as dened by the Dean of Student Life (see Section 19.5)." — is unclosed and garbled. The actual destruction date cannot be derived from the text.

Deeming an absent student to "have accepted responsibility" cannot be squared with 19.12, which places the burden of proof on the accuser, or with 19.13, which requires decisions to rest solely on evidence introduced at the hearing. Responsibility is established by non-attendance rather than proof.

Appeals lie only on "specic evidence, presented in writing" of fraud, "denial of rights under this process," procedural error, or new evidence — terms that are undefined and that exclude any challenge to the sufficiency of the evidence. "Denial of rights under this process" in particular has no stated content.

19.16 promises that a meritorious appeal produces "a new hearing of the case" before the UAB, yet 20.8 constitutes the UAB as a three-member review body and Section 23 prescribes hearing procedures only for the SCB. What a UAB "new hearing" consists of cannot be determined from the instrument.

The student has only "2 class days" from delivery of the announcement to request the meeting, and the Dean "may or may not amend" the decision under no stated standard. The review is thus a right without criteria and with a deadline running from delivery rather than receipt.

19.18 directs students to seek a continuance rather than raise a matter for the first time on appeal, which sits against 19.16.d's express appeal ground of "new evidence not previously available." Whether information glimpsed at the hearing is forfeited as an appeal ground is left to construction.

The provision says the governing procedures are those "enumerated in Section 19" but also those "available in the Department... or on the website," without saying which controls if they diverge. An off-document source is given equal standing with the handbook.

20.2 allows the mandatory panel composition to be waived only "by mutual consent of the SCB, the accuser, and the accused," whereas 19.7 allows "the accused and accuser" alone to agree to proceed without the prescribed minimum composition. The two waiver rules cannot both be applied.

"Staff members appointed by the Senior Vice President for Students and Enrollment" omits its verb, leaving it unclear whether the appointment is mandatory or merely descriptive. The provision also does not say how large the pool must be.

"A process open to all continuing students" and "a representative cross-section of Brandeis students" state no selection criteria or method, and the second sentence is syntactically scrambled. Whether a panel is properly constituted cannot be tested against these words.

"Chaired by students, each annually selected by the Board and the DSRCS Director" does not say how many chairpersons there are or how a disagreement between the Board and the Director is resolved. The plural chairs also complicate 19.13's tie-breaking rule for "the chairperson."

Removal turns on "behavior that conicts with the high standards of citizenship, condentiality, and cooperation that the Board represents," a standard with no defined content and no process. Any removal decision is effectively unreviewable on these words.

20.7 provides that "An Associate Dean of Student Life will serve as chairperson of the University Appeals Board," which cannot be squared with 20.8's requirement that "A chairperson who is a full-time tenured faculty member shall be appointed by the Dean of Student Life." The two consecutive provisions name incompatible chairs.

20.8 requires a full-time tenured faculty chairperson appointed by the Dean, while 20.7 states that an Associate Dean of Student Life will chair the UAB. Which officer presides over an appeal is left in direct conflict.

Students appointed to the Appeals Board "must be free from all elected, appointed, or afliate relationships with the Student Union or Graduate Student Association," yet the same provision has them appointed to the voter pool by the Presidents of those very bodies. The eligibility bar and the appointment mechanism work against each other.

"Selected in a manner similar to that of the SCB" imports an undefined degree of similarity to a process (20.4) that is itself unspecified. "The original appointing authority" is also ambiguous where the chair is appointed by the Dean but faculty by the Faculty Senate chair.

Removal requires consultation with "the chairperson," whose identity is itself disputed as between 20.7 and 20.8, and rests on the undefined "high standards of citizenship, condentiality, and cooperation." Neither the actor nor the standard is fixed by the text.

20.11 requires a Student Affairs administrator to be present "in all stages of the conduct process including hearings and deliberations" and to advise the Board on requirements, procedures and sanctions, which cannot be squared with 19.6's statement that the administrator "will not act in any way to inuence the outcome of a case." The same officer is given advisory power and told to have none.

The sanctioning factors are "including but not limited to" and the learning components "may include but are not limited to" a list that mixes education with "Failure in a course or on an assignment," "Restitution for damages," and "Family notication." Neither the factors nor the permissible components have any boundary.

21.1 makes sanctions effective only on approval by the Director or Associate Dean "who can modify the sanction," while 19.16 contemplates approval or modification by the Dean or the Director before appeal and empowers the UAB to increase or decrease the sanction thereafter. Who may finally set a sanction, and in what order, is stated inconsistently.

The sanction is titled "Verbal Warning" but the text describes no warning at all — only that "further action may not be deemed necessary" while the responsible finding is recorded. Whether a verbal warning is a sanction with record consequences is left ambiguous.
"Additional conditions may be applied as appropriate" places no limit on what may be attached to a written warning. The sanction is therefore open-ended despite being the second-lowest on the scale.

"Not in good standing with their living unit" is undefined and carries no stated consequence, and "conditions may be placed on their actions" is unbounded. The content of residence probation cannot be read off the provision.

"Such action would normally be taken after one serious violation or repeated violations" states a norm, not a rule, and "serious" is undefined. The provision does not say who decides or whether departure from the norm is permitted.
The privileges that may be withdrawn are "including, but not limited to" an enumerated list, so any University benefit could be swept in. "A specic period of time" is required but no maximum is set.

Probation may be revoked if the student violates its terms "or in any way fail[s] to conduct themselves as a responsible member of the University community" — a condition with no ascertainable content. Suspension or dismissal can follow on that undefined trigger.

The sentence "Suspension may extend for a semester, until a designated date, and/or until degrees/certicates will not be issued and credit will not be granted for courses taken elsewhere" is garbled and, as written, states no third alternative duration. The maximum length of a suspension cannot be determined from the text.

The University may act whenever it "has reason to believe" behavior "may pose a signicant threat" and may then "take any action that it believes to be appropriate and reasonable," with the enumerated examples expressly non-exclusive. Neither the trigger nor the permissible response has a stated limit.

22.1 authorizes removal on a "signicant threat" standard, while 22.2 provides that pending final action a student's status "shall not be altered" or campus presence suspended "except for reasons of imminent danger." The two adjacent provisions set incompatible thresholds for the same interim removal.

22.2's protection against alteration of status absent "imminent danger" cannot be squared with 22.1 ("signicant threat"), 22.3 (removal on a criminal charge), or 2.1.f and 3.0, which allow emergency suspension of any student merely accused pending investigation. The instrument states at least three different triggers for the same interim measure.

22.3 permits indefinite suspension on a mere criminal charge and declares that "the procedural standards set forth in Section 19 do not apply," which cannot be squared with 18.0's rule that discipline may be implemented "only though referral" to the DSRCS or with 22.2's imminent-danger limit. A student can be removed indefinitely with none of the process the handbook otherwise promises.

Discipline up to dismissal turns on off-campus behavior that "in the judgment of the Dean" is inconsistent with being a "good citizen[] and good neighbor[]" and "adversely affects the University community." Those standards are undefined and committed wholly to one officer's judgment.

22.4 states that "the procedural standards set forth in Section 19 do not apply" to a Dean's Sanction, which cannot be squared with 19.16's guarantee of appeal to the University Appeals Board from decisions imposing sanctions, or with 18.0's requirement of DSRCS referral. A dismissal may thus issue with no hearing and no appeal.

"Emergency protocol" is nowhere defined, yet it bars the student from all campus property and classes with "no exception for examinations or other time-sensitive... academic obligations" until the Dean gives written permission. The provision fixes no duration and no standard for lifting the protocol.

The chairperson explains a "philosophy of peer judgment" contained in a separate statement "available from the Department," a document not reproduced in the handbook. What that statement says, and whether it binds the Board, is outside the instrument.

The right "to question witnesses appearing against them" cannot be squared with 19.11, which permits the Board to receive written testimony from absentee witnesses who never appear. The stated right of confrontation is defeated by the evidentiary rule elsewhere in the instrument.

The sentence is scrambled: "bring them into the hearing room either individually or as a group for descriptions of the incident in alphabetical order" does not say whether alphabetical order governs the grouping, the descriptions, or both. "This system shall prevail throughout the remainder of the hearing procedures" then locks in whichever reading is taken.

"Witnesses for the accused may be called" is permissive, which sits against 23.C.2's statement of a right "to present witnesses on their own behalf" and 19.9's rule that testimony "may be disallowed" if a witness is not available when called. Whether the accused has a right or only a possibility of calling witnesses depends on reading the three together.

This footnote says hearing procedures "may differ" in sexual misconduct, sexual harassment, and sex discrimination cases "in accordance with Title IX" without stating how, which cannot be squared with the mandatory step-by-step procedure of Section 23 or the specific Section 3 and 7 rules in 19.13, 19.16 and 19.17. In the successor handbook such cases are removed from Section 19 entirely and sent to the Special Examiner's Process, so the footnote is the only textual hook for wholly different procedures.
"Usually within 3-5 business days" promises notification without fixing any deadline, and notice is by Brandeis e-mail only. The word "usually" makes the timing unenforceable.

The Board hears the accuser's sanction recommendation, though Section 21.0 assigns the sanctioning judgment to the DSRCS administrator or the SCB on stated factors and 19.13 has the Board recommend the sanction. The weight, if any, to be given the accuser's recommendation is unstated.

Final sanction determinations go to the accused "and in some cases to the accuser," which cannot be squared with the Section 3 services statement that "the accuser will be informed of the outcome of disciplinary proceedings in which sexual assault is alleged." One provision makes notice to the accuser discretionary, the other absolute.

The Hearing Administrator's disclosure of the accused's past conduct during deliberations cannot be squared with 19.13's requirement that "Decisions shall be based solely upon evidence and testimony introduced at the hearing," nor with 19.6's statement that the administrator will not act in any way to influence the outcome. Whether the bar applies only to the responsibility finding or also to sanctioning is left unanswered.

"The appropriate administrator" who reviews the Board's recommendations is unidentified here, while 21.1 names the Director or Associate Dean and, for suspension or dismissal, the Dean. Which officer reviews, and with what power to modify, must be assembled from other provisions.

Appeal procedures are relegated to "the nal outcome letter," a document outside the handbook, even though 19.16 already prescribes the grounds and the 7-day deadline. If the letter and 19.16 differ, nothing says which controls.
